question:
Patient note:
A 26-year-old man employed as a junior systems analyst in a municipal IT department presented to the university general-medicine clinic late this morning at the request of his new primary clinician for a comprehensive baseline evaluation before he enrolls in a demanding night-school master’s program; he wishes to ensure that several long-standing medical conditions remain stable enough to tolerate the extra workload and irregular hours. Respiratory concerns date back to early childhood, when he required nebulized bronchodilators for wheezy episodes every winter; as an adolescent he completed formal pulmonary-function testing that showed a forced expiratory volume in one second of 65 % predicted with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55 and minimal reversibility after albuterol, findings interpreted as fixed airflow limitation superimposed on atopic asthma. Since age 22 he has inhaled budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 µg two puffs twice daily and a long-acting muscarinic antagonist each morning, refilling a rescue albuterol canister roughly every six weeks when sprinting to catch commuter trains. He has never needed intubation, non-invasive ventilation, or systemic corticosteroids in the past four years, and his resting oxygen saturation today is 97 % on ambient air with respirations of 14 per minute. At 18 he was diagnosed with systemic lupus after a six-week febrile illness accompanied by malar rash, oral ulcers, arthralgia, and a high-titer antinuclear antibody of 1 : 1280; renal biopsy at that time was normal, and he has since maintained disease quiescence on hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily and sunscreen vigilance. Joints occasionally stiffen after long coding sessions but he denies morning swelling, digital ulcerations, Raynaud phenomena, serositis, or neuropsychiatric manifestations, and his most recent comprehensive metabolic panel from two weeks ago lists creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 13 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 26 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 78 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.0. Endocrine screening performed during an employee-wellness fair three years ago revealed fasting plasma glucose values of 146 and 152 mg/dL and a hemoglobin A1c of 7.6 %. He was started on metformin 1000 mg twice daily and has since logged pre-breakfast capillary glucose readings between 105 and 150 mg/dL; the laboratory report brought by the patient today shows an A1c of 7.2 % drawn last Friday. He reports no visual blurring, paresthesias, foot skin breakdown, orthostatic dizziness, or episodes of severe hypoglycemia, and a urine microalbumin-to-creatinine ratio checked one month ago measured 18 mg/g. He has never experienced crushing substernal pressure, diaphoresis out of proportion to exertion, palpitations, syncope, calf cramping while walking, unilateral weakness, transient speech disturbance, or curtain-like visual loss. He abstains from cigarettes because smoke triggers bronchospasm, drinks two craft beers on Saturday evenings, and denies recreational drug use. The patient lives with a roommate in an apartment that allows cats, owns no pets himself, bicycles five miles to work when air quality is good, and prepares most meals at home, choosing low-glycemic carbohydrates on advice of a dietitian. Family history is pertinent for a mother with well-controlled asthma, a maternal aunt with systemic lupus complicated by nephritis, and a paternal grandfather who died of pancreatic cancer at 72; no first-degree relative has suffered premature myocardial infarction or stroke. Current medications, all taken before today’s visit, include hydroxychloroquine as noted, metformin, budesonide-formoterol, tiotropium 18 µg once daily, albuterol metered-dose inhaler as needed, and a daily multivitamin; he reports a pruritic rash when prescribed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for sinusitis in high school but no other drug allergies. Review of systems is otherwise negative for fever, chills, night sweats, involuntary weight change, cough productive of purulent sputum or blood, hematuria, abdominal pain, melena, dyspepsia, jaundice, skin ulcerations, unexplained bruising, lymph-node enlargement, or headache. Vital signs after a five-minute seated rest read: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg in the right arm, pulse 78 beats per minute regular, respiratory rate as noted, oxygen saturation 97 % on room air, weight 74 kg, height 180 cm, body-mass index 22.8 kg/m². He appears well nourished, speaks in full sentences without accessory-muscle use, and demonstrates no photosensitive rash today. Conjunctivae are pink, sclerae anicteric; oral mucosa is moist with no ulcerations. Neck is supple with no lymphadenopathy and brisk carotid upstrokes without bruit. Jugular venous pulsation is 2 cm above the sternal angle at 45°. Cardiac apex is non-displaced, S1 and S2 are crisp without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs are hyper-resonant to percussion with prolonged expiratory phase and scattered end-expiratory wheezes but no crackles. Abdomen is flat, nontender, with active bowel sounds and no organomegaly. Extremities are warm with radial and dorsalis pedis pulses 2+/4 symmetrical, no edema, and capillary refill under two seconds. Musculoskeletal exam reveals full active range of motion in wrists, elbows, shoulders, knees, and ankles without synovitis or effusion; grip strength is symmetric. Neurologic screening shows an alert, oriented individual with fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength throughout, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, symmetric deep-tendon reflexes, and steady tandem gait. Skin inspection finds scattered hyperpigmented macules from childhood varicella but no livedo, palpable purpura, or digital infarcts. A point-of-care glucometer immediately before examination registers 138 mg/dL. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram recorded in clinic shows normal sinus rhythm at 80 beats per minute, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 90 ms, axis 20°, and no pathologic Q waves or ST-segment deviations. The patient seeks guidance on timing of inhalers around evening classes, strategies to minimize glucose variability when meals are delayed, and appropriate frequency of rheumatology follow-up while his lupus remains clinically quiet.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums the weights of qualifying baseline conditions.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: 1 point for asthma with persistent airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC 0.55) requiring daily inhalers.
- Connective tissue disease: 1 point for systemic lupus, even though it is clinically quiet.
- Diabetes without documented end-organ damage: 1 point. He takes metformin, has a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 18 mg/g, and has no documented retinopathy or neuropathy.
- Age 26: 0 age-adjustment points. No other qualifying condition is documented.
Total: 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 3.
Final answer: 3
